Context: the spec (source of truth) is /root/bench-runs/h4-c3e12a23/.team/notes/spec.md — read the "Server" section. The server is /root/bench-runs/h4-c3e12a23/server.mjs (read it only to understand, never change it). Use the harness /root/bench-runs/h4-c3e12a23/test/helpers/server-harness.mjs (read it): `makeTempDir`, `removeDir`, `runUntilExit({env, cwd})` → {code, signal, stdout, stderr}, `startServer({env, cwd})` → {port, output, isRunning, stop} (PORT defaults to '0'; pass `PORT: undefined` to leave it unset), `request(port, {method, path, headers, body})`, `postBooking(port, obj)`, `validBooking(overrides)`. Always spawn with cwd = a fresh temp dir; clean up in after/finally; always stop servers.

Project rules: small focused functions (<50 lines), no console.log, exact equality assertions (assert.equal / deepEqual on the whole value, never regex/prefix for values the spec names), table-driven tests where it fits, each test name says the spec behaviour.

Define a helper `assertOneStderrLineExit1(result)`: code === 1, stdout === '', stderr matches /^[^\n]+\n$/ (exactly one line) and does not contain '    at ' (no stack trace).

Tests to write:
1. Invalid PORT, each of: 'abc', '-1', '+80', ' 80', '80 ', '65536', '99999', '1e3', '0x50', '8.0', '٣' (Arabic-indic digit), '１' (fullwidth): assertOneStderrLineExit1. Use a valid empty data dir.
2. PORT check comes before data file read: PORT='abc' with DATA_FILE pointing to a directory (create subdir 'dir') → exit 1, one line, and stderr !== 'cannot read data file dir\n'.
3. Port in use: occupy a port with `net.createServer().listen(0,'127.0.0.1')`, spawn with that PORT → assertOneStderrLineExit1; close the blocker.
4. Data file read comes before listening: bad data file (directory) + PORT in use → stderr exactly `cannot read data file <name>\n`, exit 1.
5. PORT='0' → stdout is exactly `listening on http://127.0.0.1:${port}\n` (whole stdout string equality), and the port really answers GET /api/rooms with 200. After a few requests (GET, POST 201, 404, 400), stdout is still exactly that one line.
6. PORT unset and PORT='' → listens on 3000: stdout exactly 'listening on http://127.0.0.1:3000\n'. Run these two sequentially in one test. If port 3000 is already busy on the machine (probe with net first), call t.skip('port 3000 busy').
7. PORT='00000' is digits only → valid (port 0 → OS picks), stdout matches the listening line with a nonzero port. Also PORT='65535'... skip that (may be busy); instead test that a free high port given with leading zero e.g. find a free port P via net, then PORT='0'+P → listening line exactly with port P.
8. DATA_FILE default: DATA_FILE unset, cwd=temp → POST valid booking → file `<tmp>/bookings.json` exists and parses to an object; DATA_FILE='' same. Also relative DATA_FILE 'sub/data.json' (mkdir sub) resolves against cwd: file `<tmp>/sub/data.json` exists after POST, and NOT next to server.mjs (assert /root/bench-runs/h4-c3e12a23/sub does not exist and the repo has no new bookings.json — check before/after existence of /root/bench-runs/h4-c3e12a23/bookings.json is unchanged).
9. ENOENT → empty: DATA_FILE='missing.json' → GET /api/bookings → {bookings: []}; DATA_FILE='nofolder/deeper/x.json' (folders missing) → starts, empty list, and after the GETs the folder 'nofolder' still does not exist.
10. Unreadable/wrong data → exact stderr `cannot read data file <name as given>\n`, exit 1, stdout '' (not listening). Table: path is a directory; empty file; 'not json'; '{'; 'null'; '[]'; '{}'; '"x"'; '{"nextId":1}'; '{"bookings":[]}'; '{"nextId":1,"bookings":[],"extra":1}'; '{"nextId":"1","bookings":[]}'; '{"nextId":2,"bookings":[{"id":1,"room":"Nope","title":"t","date":"2026-11-03","start":"09:00","end":"10:00"}]}'. Use DATA_FILE names given in different forms: plain 'data.json', './data.json', 'sub/../data.json', and an absolute path — in each case stderr must contain the name exactly as given (e.g. `cannot read data file ./data.json\n`). Also DATA_FILE unset with cwd containing an invalid bookings.json → `cannot read data file bookings.json\n`; DATA_FILE='' same text.
11. Valid file written in the server's layout `{"nextId":1,"bookings":[]}` starts fine (sanity).

Run `cd /root/bench-runs/h4-c3e12a23 && node --test test/server-startup.test.mjs` until it passes against the real server. If a test fails and you believe the SERVER violates the spec, do not change the server or weaken the test: report it clearly (test name, expected, actual). content.content: 1 # Full spec (verbatim from user) — owner: supervisor — 2026-11-02 2 3 AUTOMATED BENCHMARK TASK. No human will answer questions: the requirements below are complete and final. Use only Node.js built-ins (no npm install). Do not use the Fable model. The project's own tests must pass at the end. 4 5 Build a meeting-room booking app: an HTTP server `server.mjs` (an ES module, run as `node server.mjs`) that serves a JSON API and a browser page, and keeps its data in one JSON file. 6 7 Server 8 - At startup the server checks `PORT`, then reads the data file, then starts listening, in that order. 9 - It listens on 127.0.0.1 at the port in the `PORT` environment variable. An unset or empty `PORT` means 3000. A `PORT` that is not made only of ASCII digits 0-9, or whose value is above 65535, or a port that cannot be bound (for example because it is in use), makes the server write one line of its choice to stderr and exit with code 1. 10 - Once listening, it prints `listening on http://127.0.0.1:` followed by "\n" to stdout, where `` is the port actually bound (with `PORT=0`, the port the OS picked). This line is the only thing the server ever writes to stdout. 11 - Its data lives in the file named by the `DATA_FILE` environment variable, as JSON in a layout of your choice. An unset or empty `DATA_FILE` means `bookings.json`. A relative `DATA_FILE`, the default included, is resolved against the current working directory, not the folder of `server.mjs`. 12 - The server reads the data file once, at startup. If reading it fails with `ENOENT` (the file, or a folder on its path, does not exist), there are no bookings yet. If reading it fails in any other way (for example the path is a directory), or its content is not data in the layout this server writes (for example it is empty or not valid JSON), the server writes `cannot read data file ` followed by "\n" to stderr, where `` is the value of `DATA_FILE` as given (`bookings.json` when it is unset or empty), and exits with code 1 without listening. 13 - After startup the server's memory is the truth: changes made to the file from outside are not noticed. The server writes the data file only when a POST creates a booking or a DELETE removes one, never at startup or for any other request, and it never creates folders. 14 - Every change is saved to the data file before its reply is sent: after a restart with the same `DATA_FILE`, the bookings, and the id the next booking will get, are as before. 15 - If saving a change fails (for example because the data file's folder does not exist), the reply is 500 `internal error` and nothing changes, the next id included. Any other unexpected failure while handling a request also replies 500 `internal error`. In both cases the server keeps running. 16 - Requests that arrive at the same time give the same result as if they had been handled one at a time in some order: of several overlapping bookings sent at once while saving works, exactly one is created and every other one gets 409, and no id is given twice. 17 - Before sending any reply, the server reads the whole request body, if there is one, and discards what it does not use, so the client always receives the reply, the 413 and 415 replies included. 18 19 API 20 - The rooms are fixed: `Aurora`, `Borealis` and `Cosmos`, in that order. 21 - A booking is a JSON object with exactly the keys `id`, `room`, `title`, `date`, `start` and `end`: `id` is a number, the others are strings. The first booking gets id 1 and each new booking the next integer; an id is never reused, even after deletes and restarts. 22 - Only the parsed JSON of a reply body matters: whitespace and key order in it are free. 23 - A request's path is its request target up to the first `?` (all of it when there is no `?`). Routes compare the path byte for byte, with no percent-decoding and no dot-segment, slash or letter-case normalisation: `/api/%62ookings`, `/api/./rooms`, `/API/rooms` and `/api/bookings/` are none of the paths below. The query, the text after the first `?`, is ignored unless stated, and is decoded as `new URLSearchParams(query)` does. 24 - `GET /api/rooms`: 200 `{"rooms": ["Aurora", "Borealis", "Cosmos"]}`. 25 - `GET /api/bookings`: 200 `{"bookings": [...]}` with every booking, sorted by date, then start, then room in the order above. When the query has a `date` parameter (as `params.has('date')` says; `?date` with no `=` counts, with the empty value), its value is `params.get('date')` (the first one when repeated) and the reply holds only the bookings on that date; a value that is not a valid date by rule 6 below (the empty value included) gets 400 `date must be a valid YYYY-MM-DD date`. Other query parameters are ignored. 26 - `POST /api/bookings` with a JSON body holding `room`, `title`, `date`, `start` and `end`: 201 and the new booking. Other keys in the body are ignored. 27 - `DELETE /api/bookings/`: every path that is `/api/bookings/` followed by a non-empty `` holding no `/` is this route, whatever `` is.
